rules.name: Five boxes a screen
rules.statement: Every screen of the map should hold between three and nine boxes. Five is the number it aims for.
rules.risk: A screen packed with boxes buries the product, so the reader stops drilling and never finds what it does.

sites.why: states the target of five boxes a screen and the readable range of three to nine
counts a screen as reading well only when its box count falls inside that range
marks a screen holding ten boxes or more as past the readable range

rules.name: Same-kind lists read dense
rules.statement: A screen whose boxes are all the same kind reads as a list, so fifteen boxes are fine there.
rules.risk: Cutting a plain list into invented groups adds levels that name nothing a reader was looking for.

sites.why: grants the one exemption, for a screen of same-kind neighbours sharing a folder or a name ending
holds back the crowded-screen advice for such a screen until it passes fifteen boxes
labels the same screen exempt in the report instead of crowded

rules.name: Thin screens count only at the top
rules.statement: Only the first screen is faulted for holding too few boxes. A screen deeper down may be small.
rules.risk: A first screen of two boxes tells the reader the technology used, never what the product does.

sites.why: says too few boxes is a fault at the first screen only, and normal deeper down
raises the too-few-boxes advice for the first screen and for no other
names the thin deeper screens in the report while saying they are not a fault

rules.name: One-child levels earn nothing
rules.statement: A group holding exactly one thing is reported, because that level costs a click and adds no meaning.
rules.risk: Wrapper levels push what the reader came for one click further down for nothing in return.

sites.why: names a group with one member as a level pulling no weight, to be removed or grown
reports a group whose single member is one box rather than another group
reports a group whose single member is another group of the same kind

rules.name: Crowding advises, never blocks
rules.statement: A crowded or thin screen is only ever advice. It never refuses a map or stops a build.
rules.risk: Refusing a map over a box count pushes a builder to invent groups that fit the number.

sites.why: states that screen density never refuses a map, because grouping is a free choice about the picture
files every screen-density finding as advice rather than as a fault that refuses the map
records the density findings in the closing report without moving its verdict

rules.name: Regrouping never resizes boxes
rules.statement: Regrouping may only move boxes between groups. It may never merge or split the boxes themselves.
rules.risk: Merging boxes to fix a crowded screen makes the map say the code holds fewer parts than it does.

sites.why: forbids any density finding from merging or splitting boxes to reach a number
writes a split suggestion as a change of which group a box sits in, and nothing else
tells the reader applying a suggestion to add no member the suggestion did not list

rules.name: Groups carry no arrows
rules.statement: A group is never one end of an arrow, so moving a box into another group moves no arrow.
rules.risk: An arrow leaving a whole group cannot be drawn on any one screen, so the picture stops making sense.

sites.why: says dissolving a level moves no arrow, because a group is never an end of one
refuses a map holding any arrow that starts or ends at a group

rules.name: Grouping starts above fifteen boxes
rules.statement: Grouping is worth doing only once a map passes about fifteen boxes. A smaller map stays flat.
rules.risk: Groups on a small map add levels the reader must click through to reach a list they could already see.

sites.why: makes groups optional, and recommends them only above about fifteen boxes
asks for groups only once an ungrouped map passes that count
